title: yq: Reading and Editing YAML Without sed
intro: Pipelines constantly need to change one value in a YAML file: an image tag, a replica count. Doing it with sed works until the indentation or a comment changes, and then it silently edits the wrong line or nothing at all. yq understands the structure. (This is the Go yq by Mike Farah, the common one; its syntax is close to jq's.) You have values.yaml and deployment.yaml.

steps.prompt: Read the replica count from deployment.yaml.
steps.why: The path is the same dotted form as in jq and in kubectl's jsonpath. Reading a value this way is safe against reformatting, where 'grep replicas' would also match 'minReplicas' or a comment.

steps.prompt: List the image of every container in deployment.yaml.
steps.explanation: Two containers: the app and a sidecar.
steps.why: '[]' iterates a list, as in jq. This is the check to run before a scripted image update: there are two images here, and a naive 'replace the image line' would change the wrong one or both.

steps.prompt: Set image.tag to 1.8.3 in values.yaml, editing the file in place.
steps.fake_output:
(no output: values.yaml updated)

image:
  repository: registry.example.com/shop
  tag: "1.8.3"   # bumped by CI
steps.explanation: Only that value changed; the comment and the rest of the file are intact.
steps.why: This is the line a pipeline runs to promote a build in a GitOps repository. yq keeps comments and key order, so the commit's diff is one line. Quote the value: an unquoted 1.8 would be written as a number, and Helm would then render the tag '1.8' or even '1.80' differently from what you meant.

steps.prompt: The file all.yaml contains many Kubernetes documents separated by ---. Print the names of the ones whose kind is Deployment.
steps.why: yq applies the expression to each document in a multi-document file. That makes it the tool for inspecting 'helm template' or 'kubectl kustomize' output: pick out one kind, check a field across all of them, or count them, before anything is applied.

steps.prompt: Convert values.yaml to JSON, so jq or another tool can take it from there.
steps.why: YAML is a superset of JSON, so conversion loses only comments. It's also a quick way to see what a YAML file really means: surprises such as 'no' parsed as false, or a version parsed as a number, are obvious in the JSON. '-P' goes the other way, pretty-printing JSON as YAML.
